must permit another person to inspect, at all reasonable times, such (if any) of the books as the other person would be entitled to inspect if they were not in the authorised officer’s possession; and
may permit another person to inspect any of the books.
Unless subparagraph (1)(b)(ii) applies, the authorised officer may deliver any of the books into the possession of the Registrar or a person approved by the Registrar to receive them.

If paragraph (1)(a) or (b) applies, the authorised officer, the Registrar or an approved person into whose possession the authorised officer delivers any of the books under subsection (8), may require:
if paragraph (1)(a) applies—a person who so produced any of the books; or
in any case—a person who was a party to the compilation of any of the books;
to explain any matter about the compilation of any of the books or to which any of the books relate.
Subsection (9) does not apply to the extent that the person has explained the matter to the best of his or her knowledge or belief.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matter in subsection (10) (see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code).
A person must not intentionally or recklessly fail to comply with a requirement under subsection (9).
Penalty: 100 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.
Subsection (11) does not apply to the extent to which the person has a reasonable excuse.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matter in subsection (12) (see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code).

subDivision.heading: Warrants by telephone or other electronic means

section.heading: Applying for warrants by telephone or other electronic means

content.p: The Registrar or an authorised officer may apply to a magistrate for a warrant by telephone, fax or other electronic means:
in an urgent case; or
if the delay that would occur if an application were made in person would frustrate the effective execution of the warrant.
An application under subsection (1):
must include all information that would be required in an ordinary application for a warrant; and
if necessary, may be made before the information is sworn or affirmed.
The magistrate may require:
communication by voice to the extent that it is practicable in the circumstances; and
any further information.
The function of issuing a warrant is conferred on the magistrate in a personal capacity and not as a court or a member of a court. The magistrate need not accept the function conferred.
The magistrate may complete and sign the same form of warrant that would be issued under section 456-5 if satisfied that:
a warrant in the terms of the application should be issued urgently; or
the delay that would occur if an application were made in person would frustrate the effective execution of the warrant.

If the magistrate issues the warrant, he or she must inform the applicant, by telephone, fax or other electronic means, of the terms of the warrant and the day on which and the time at which it was signed.
The applicant must then:
complete a form of warrant in terms substantially corresponding to those given by the magistrate; and
state on the form:
the name of the magistrate; and
the day on which the warrant was signed; and
the time at which the warrant was signed.
The applicant must give the magistrate:
the form of warrant completed by the applicant; and
if the information was unsworn under paragraph 456-15(2)(b)—the sworn information;
by the end of the day after whichever first occurs:
the warrant expires; or
the warrant is executed.
The magistrate must attach the form of warrant completed by the magistrate to the documents provided under subsection (4).

section.heading: Unsigned warrants by telephone etc. in court proceedings

content.p: If:
it is material, in any proceedings, for a court to be satisfied that the exercise of a power under a warrant issued under this Division was duly authorised; and
the form of warrant signed by the magistrate is not produced in evidence;
the court must assume that the exercise of the power was not duly authorised unless the contrary is proved.

subDivision.heading: Offences relating to warrants by telephone or other electronic means

section.heading: Offence for stating incorrect names in warrants by telephone etc.

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person states a name of a magistrate in a document; and
the document purports to be a form of warrant under section 456-20; and
the name is not the name of the magistrate who issued the warrant.
Penalty: 120 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.

section.heading: Offence for unauthorised form of warrant

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person states a matter in a form of warrant under section 456-20; and
the matter departs in a material particular from the form authorised by the magistrate.
Penalty: 120 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.

section.heading: Offence for execution etc. of unauthorised form of warrant

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person executes a document or presents a document to a person; and
the document purports to be a form of warrant under section 456-20; and
the document:
has not been approved by a magistrate under that section; or
departs in a material particular from the terms authorised by the magistrate under that section.
Penalty: 120 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.

section.heading: Offence for giving unexecuted form of warrant

content.p: A person commits an offence if:
the person gives a magistrate a form of warrant under section 456-20; and
the document is not the form of warrant that the person executed.
Penalty: 120 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.

subDivision.heading: Warrant details to be given to occupier

section.heading: Details of warrant to be given to occupier etc.

content.p: If a warrant in relation to premises is being executed and the occupier of the premises or another person who apparently represents the occupier is present at the premises, the authorised officer executing the warrant must make available to that person a copy of the warrant.
The authorised officer must identify himself or herself to the person at the premises.
The copy of the warrant referred to in subsection (1) need not include the signature of the issuing magistrate or the seal of the relevant court.

part.heading: Offences relating to regulatory and enforcement powers of Registrar

division.heading: Offences relating to regulatory and enforcement powers of Registrar

section.heading: Obstructing Registrar or interfering with meeting called by Registrar etc.

content.p: A person must not:
engage in conduct that results in the obstruction or hindering of an authorised officer in the performance of the officer’s powers under Part 10-3; or
engage in conduct that results in the obstruction or hindering of a person who is executing a warrant under Division 456.
Penalty: 100 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the extent that the person has a reasonable excuse.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matters in subsection (2) (see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code).

The occupier, or person in charge, of premises that a person enters under a warrant issued under Division 456 must not intentionally or recklessly fail to provide to that person all reasonable facilities and assistance for the effective exercise of his or her powers under the warrant.
Penalty: 25 penalty units or imprisonment for 6 months, or both.
A person must not:
engage in conduct that results in the obstruction or hindering of the Registrar or the Registrar’s delegate in the performance or exercise of any of the Registrar’s functions and powers; or
engage in conduct that results in the disruption of a meeting called under section 439-10 or 439-15.
Penalty: 50 penalty units or imprisonment for 1 year, or both.
An offence constituted by a contravention of subsection (4) is punishable on summary conviction.
A person must not, in purported compliance with a requirement made under Part 10-3, give information, or make a statement, that is false or misleading in a material particular.
Penalty: 100 penalty units or imprisonment for 2 years, or both.

It is a defence to a prosecution for a contravention of subsection (1) if it is proved that the defendant, when giving the information or evidence or making the statement, believed on reasonable grounds that it was true and not misleading.
Note: A defendant bears a legal burden in relation to the matter in subsection (3) (see section 13.4 of the Criminal Code).
If a requirement under section 453-1 or 453-5 has been made to produce a book, a person must not:
in any case—engage in conduct that results in the concealment, destruction, mutilation or alteration of the book; or
if a book is in a particular State or Territory—engage in conduct that results in the taking or sending of the book out of that State or Territory or out of Australia.
Penalty: 200 penalty units or imprisonment for 5 years, or both.
It is a defence to a prosecution for a contravention of subsection (1) if it is proved that the defendant did not intend to defeat the purposes of this Act.
Note: A defendant bears a legal burden in relation to a matter mentioned in subsection (2) (see section 13.4 of the Criminal Code).
For the purposes of Part 10-3, it is not a reasonable excuse for a person to refuse or fail:
to give information; or
to produce a book;
in accordance with a requirement made of the person, that the information or production of the book, as the case may be, might tend to incriminate the person or make the person liable to a penalty.
Subsection (3) applies if:

before making an oral statement giving information in compliance with a requirement made under this Part or Part 10-3, a person (other than a body corporate) claims that the statement might tend to incriminate the person or make the person liable to a penalty; and
the statement might in fact tend to incriminate the person or make the person so liable.
The statement is not admissible in evidence against the person in:
a criminal proceeding; or
a proceeding for the imposition of a penalty;
other than a proceeding in respect of the falsity of the statement.

division.heading: Which disclosures qualify for protection under this Part?

content.p: (1) A disclosure of information by a person (the discloser) qualifies for protection under this Part if:
the discloser is:
an officer or contact person of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; or
an employee of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; or
a person who has a contract for the supply of services or goods to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; or
an employee of a person who has a contract for the supply of services or goods to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
the disclosure is made to:
the Registrar; or
the corporation’s auditor or a member of an audit team conducting an audit of the corporation; or
a director, secretary or senior manager of the corporation; or
a person authorised by the corporation to receive disclosures of that kind; and
the discloser informs the person to whom the disclosure is made of the discloser’s name before making the disclosure; and
the discloser has reasonable grounds to suspect that the information indicates that:
the corporation has, or may have, contravened a provision of this Act; or
an officer or employee of the corporation has, or may have, contravened a provision of this Act; and
the discloser makes the disclosure in good faith.
A reference in subsection (1) to a person contravening a provision of this Act includes a reference to a person committing an offence against, or based on, a provision of this Act.
Note: This subsection causes section 11.6 of the Criminal Code to operate in relation to such references.

section.heading: Disclosure that qualifies for protection not actionable etc.

content.p: If a person makes a disclosure that qualifies for protection under this Part:
the person is not subject to any civil or criminal liability for making the disclosure; and
no contractual or other remedy may be enforced, and no contractual or other right may be exercised, against the person on the basis of the disclosure.
Note: This subsection does not provide that the person is not subject to any civil or criminal liability for conduct of the person that is revealed by the disclosure.
Without limiting subsection (1):
the person has qualified privilege in respect of the disclosure; and
a contract to which the person is a party may not be terminated on the basis that the disclosure constitutes a breach of the contract.
Without limiting paragraphs (1)(b) and (2)(b), if a court is satisfied that:
(a) a person (the employee) is employed in a particular position under a contract of employment with another person (the employer); and
the employee makes a disclosure that qualifies for protection under this Part; and
the employer purports to terminate the contract of employment on the basis of the disclosure;
the court may order that the employee be reinstated in that position or a position at a comparable level.
Actually causing detriment to another person
(1) A person (the first person) contravenes this subsection if:
the first person engages in conduct; and
(b) the first person’s conduct causes any detriment to another person (the second person); and
the first person intends that his or her conduct cause detriment to the second person; and
the first person engages in his or her conduct because the second person or a third person made a disclosure that qualifies for protection under this Part.
Penalty: 25 penalty units or imprisonment for 6 months, or both.
Threatening to cause detriment to another person
(2) A person (the first person) contravenes this subsection if:
(a) the first person makes to another person (the second person) a threat to cause any detriment to the second person or to a third person; and
the first person:
intends the second person to fear that the threat will be carried out; or
is reckless as to causing the second person to fear that the threat will be carried out; and
the first person makes the threat because a person:
makes a disclosure that qualifies for protection under this Part; or
may make a disclosure that would qualify for protection under this Part.
Penalty: 25 penalty units or imprisonment for 6 months, or both.
Officers and employees involved in contravention

If an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation contravenes subsection (1) or (2), any officer or employee of the corporation who is involved in that contravention contravenes this subsection.
Penalty: 25 penalty units or imprisonment for 6 months, or both.
Threats
For the purposes of subsection (2), a threat may be:
express or implied; or
conditional or unconditional.
In a prosecution for an offence against subsection (2), it is not necessary to prove that the person threatened actually feared that the threat would be carried out.
If:
(a) a person (the person in contravention) contravenes subsection 469-5(1), (2) or (3); and
(b) a person (the victim) suffers damage because of the contravention;
the person in contravention is liable to compensate the victim for the damage.

section.heading: Confidentiality requirements for corporations, corporation officers and employees and auditors

content.p: (1) A person (the offender) commits an offence against this subsection if:
(a) a person (the discloser) makes a disclosure of information (the qualifying disclosure) that qualifies for protection under this Part; and
the qualifying disclosure relates to a contravention or possible contravention of a provision of this Act by:
an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; or
an officer or employee of the corporation; and
the qualifying disclosure is made to:
the corporation’s auditor or a member of an audit team conducting an audit of the corporation; or
a director, secretary or senior manager of the corporation; or
a person authorised by the corporation to receive disclosures of that kind; and
the offender is:
the corporation’s auditor or a member of an audit team conducting an audit of the corporation; or
a director, secretary or senior manager of the corporation; or
a person authorised by the corporation to receive disclosures of that kind; or
the corporation; or
any officer or employee of the corporation; and
(e) the offender discloses one of the following (the confidential information):
the information disclosed in the qualifying disclosure;
the identity of the discloser;
information that is likely to lead to the identification of the discloser; and
the confidential information is information that the offender obtained directly or indirectly because of the qualifying disclosure; and
either:
the offender is the person to whom the qualifying disclosure is made; or

the offender is a person to whom the confidential information is disclosed in contravention of this section and the offender knows that the disclosure of the confidential information to the offender was unlawful or made in breach of confidence; and
the disclosure referred to in paragraph (e) is not authorised under subsection (2).
Penalty: 25 penalty units.
The disclosure referred to in paragraph (1)(e) is authorised under this subsection if it:
is made to:
the Registrar; or
ASIC; or
the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority; or
(b) is made to a member or special member of the Australian Federal Police (within the meaning of the Australian Federal Police Act 1979); or
is made to a member (however described) of a police force of a State or Territory; or
is made to someone else with the consent of the discloser.

This Chapter deals with the various ways in which the management of some or all of the affairs of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation may be assumed by someone other than the directors of the corporation.
There are basically 5 ways in which this can happen:
The Registrar may appoint a special administrator for the corporation under Part 11-2.
A receiver, or another controller, of the corporation’s property may be appointed under the provisions of Part 5.2 of the Corporations Act (as applied by Part 11-3 of this Act).
An administrator for the corporation may be appointed under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by Part 11-4 of this Act).
A restructuring practitioner for the corporation may be appointed under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by Part 11-4A of this Act).
The corporation may be wound up on the grounds set out in Part 11-5 of this Act (with the winding up being carried out under Chapter 5 of the Corporations Act as applied by Part 11-5 of this Act).
The following Parts of this Chapter also apply some other provisions of the Corporations Act to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation:
Part 11-6 applies Divisions 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Part 5.7B of the Corporations Act (which deal with insolvent trading and creditor-defeating dispositions);
Part 11-7 applies Part 5.8A of the Corporations Act (which deals with employee entitlements).

division.heading: Special administration of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

section.heading: Registrar may put Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation under special administration

content.p: The Registrar may determine, in writing, that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to be under special administration for the period specified in the determination.
A determination under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
The Registrar:
must not make a determination under subsection (1) if:
the corporation is being wound up; or
a liquidator of the corporation has been appointed; and
may make a determination under subsection (1) even if the corporation is:
being administered under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act); or
under restructuring under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act).
The Registrar may make a determination under subsection (1) only if the Registrar is satisfied that at least one of the grounds set out in section 487-5 is satisfied.
The Registrar must make a determination under subsection (1) in accordance with section 487-10.
The following are the grounds for determining that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to be under special administration:
the corporation has traded at a loss for at least 6 months during the period of 12 months before the determination is made;
the corporation or the officers of the corporation have failed to comply with, or to ensure that the corporation complies with, one or more of the following:
a provision of this Act;
an internal governance rule of the corporation;
a notice that the Registrar has given the directors under section 439-20;
and the corporation has, or the officers have, failed to give the Registrar a satisfactory explanation for the failure;
the corporation has failed to comply with an obligation under Part 7-3;
if the corporation is a registered native title body corporate—there has been a serious failure, or a number of failures, by the corporation to comply with its Native Title legislation obligations;
the officers of the corporation have acted in the affairs of the corporation:
in their own interests rather than in the interests of the members of the corporation as a whole; or
in a way that appears to be unfair or unjust to members of the corporation;
the affairs of the corporation are being conducted in a way that is:
oppressive; or
unfairly prejudicial to, or unfairly discriminatory against, a member or members of the corporation; or
contrary to the interests of the members of the corporation as a whole;
disputes between:
the corporation’s members; or
the corporation’s members and the corporation’s officers;
are interfering with the proper conduct of the corporation’s affairs;
disputes between the corporation’s officers are interfering with the proper conduct of the corporation’s affairs;
a majority of the corporation’s directors have requested the Registrar in writing to appoint a special administrator;
at least the required number of members under subsection (4) request the Registrar, in writing, to appoint a special administrator;
the appointment of the special administrator is otherwise required:
in the interests of the members of the corporation; or
in the interest of the corporation’s creditors; or
in the public interest.
A paragraph in this subsection does not limit any of the other paragraphs in this subsection.

Paragraph (1)(d) or (e) does not apply to an officer of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is a registered native title body corporate merely because of doing (or refraining from doing) a particular act if the officer does (or refrains from doing) the act:
in good faith; and
with the belief that doing (or refraining from doing) the act is necessary to ensure that the corporation complies with a Native Title legislation obligation.
Separate copies of a document setting out a request under paragraph (1)(i) may be used for signing by members if the wording of the request is identical in each copy.
The required number of members for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is the greater of:
5 members of the corporation; or
10% of the members of the corporation.
The regulations may prescribe a different number of members for the purposes of applying paragraph (4)(a) to:
a particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; or
a particular class of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation.
The regulations may prescribe a different percentage for the purposes of applying paragraph (4)(b) to:
a particular Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; or
a particular class of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation.
Subject to subsection (2), the Registrar must, before determining that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to be under special administration:
give the corporation notice in writing inviting the corporation to show cause, within a reasonable period specified in the notice, why the determination should not be made; and
consider any representations the corporation makes to the Registrar within that period.
Subsection (1) does not apply if the Registrar is satisfied that the determination needs to be made as a matter of urgency to prevent:
a likely loss of property of the corporation; or
a likely loss of public money held or administered by the corporation; or
conduct that would contravene:
a provision of this Act or the regulations; or
a law of the Commonwealth or a State or Territory; or
the corporation ceasing to provide, or suspending the provision of, services that are essential to, or very significant for, a particular community or group.
(3) Public money includes money that:
has been granted to the corporation by:
the Commonwealth, a State or a Territory; or
a public authority; and
has been granted to the corporation on conditions.
Without limiting paragraph (2)(c), the conduct referred to in that paragraph may be conduct of:
the corporation; or
an officer of the corporation; or
a body corporate related to the corporation; or
an officer of a body corporate related to the corporation.
If the Registrar:
gives an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation notice under subsection (1); and
decides not to proceed to determine that the corporation is to be under special administration;

the Registrar must give the corporation notice in writing, as soon as practicable after the decision is made, that the Registrar does not propose to determine that the corporation is to be under special administration.

section.heading: Extension of period of special administration

content.p: The Registrar may extend the period for which an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to be under special administration.
An extension under subsection (1) must:
be made in writing; and
be made before the period to be extended ends.
The Registrar may determine in writing that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to cease to be under special administration on the date specified in the determination.
A determination under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.

Without limiting subsection (1), the Registrar may determine that the corporation is to cease to be under special administration if the Registrar is satisfied that it is no longer necessary for the corporation to be under special administration.

section.heading: References to corporation under special administration

content.p: If the Registrar determines under subsection 487-1(1) in relation to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation, the corporation:
(a) starts being under special administration when the period specified in the determination under subsection 487-1(1) starts; and
(b) ceases being under special administration:
when the period specified in the determination under subsection 487-1(1), or that period as extended under section 487-15, ends; or

if, before the end of the period referred to in subparagraph (i), a liquidator for the corporation is appointed, or the winding up of the corporation starts, as a result of an application made by the Registrar or the special administrator—when the liquidator is appointed or the winding up starts; or
if, before the end of the period referred to in subparagraph (i), the Registrar makes a determination under section 487-20—on the date specified in the determination under section 487-20.

Note: Subparagraph (b)(ii)—once the corporation is under special administration only the Registrar or the special administrator can apply for the winding up of the corporation (see subsection 526-15(3)).
The Registrar may appoint a special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration.

Note: The special administrator may be appointed either as the initial special administrator for the special administration of the corporation or to replace a special administrator who was appointed earlier.
The appointment must be made in writing.
The appointment must specify the period for which the special administrator is appointed.
The Registrar may extend the period for which a special administrator is appointed.
An extension under subsection (2) must:
be made in writing; and
be made before the period to be extended ends.
An appointment:
has effect, subject to paragraph (b), until the end of the period of the appointment; and
ceases to have effect if it is terminated under section 505-1 before the end of that period.

section.heading: Notice of special administration determination or appointment of special administrator

content.p: This section applies if the Registrar makes any of the following decisions:
a determination under section 487-1 that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to be under special administration;
an appointment under section 490-1 of a special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation;
an extension under section 487-15 of the period for which an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to be under special administration;
an extension under section 490-5 of the period for which a special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is appointed;
a determination under section 487-20 that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to cease to be under special administration.
The Registrar must, as soon as practicable, give notice of the decision to:
the corporation; and
any receiver, or receiver and manager, of property of the corporation of whom the Registrar is aware.
A notice under subsection (2) is not a legislative instrument.
The Registrar must, as soon as practicable, publish a notice of the decision:
(a) in the Gazette; and
either:
in a national newspaper; or

for each State or Territory in which the corporation has its registered office (if any) or carries on business or other operations—in a daily newspaper that circulates generally in that State or Territory.
The notice under subsection (2) or (4) must specify:
the period for which the corporation is to be under special administration; or
the period for which the special administrator is appointed; or
the period for which the special administration is extended; or
the period for which the appointment of the special administrator is extended; or
the date on which the corporation is to cease to be under special administration.

division.heading: Effect of appointment of special administrator on officers of the corporation

section.heading: General rule that offices of directors and secretary vacated when special administrator appointed

content.p: Subject to section 496-5, the following offices become vacant on the appointment of a special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation:
the office of each director of the corporation;
the office of each secretary (if any) of the corporation.
Subsection (1) applies even if the special administrator is appointed to replace another special administrator for the corporation.

Note: This subsection has the effect that if a special administrator is appointed and the Registrar determines, as part of that appointment, that the offices of the corporation’s officers are not to be vacated, the subsequent appointment of a replacement special administrator will automatically vacate those offices unless a fresh determination is made under section 496-5 in relation to the new appointment.

section.heading: Registrar may determine that offices not vacated in certain circumstances

content.p: The Registrar:
may determine that the offices of the corporation’s directors are not vacated on the appointment of a special administrator; and
may determine that the office of the corporation’s secretary is not vacated, or the offices of each of the corporation’s secretaries are not vacated, on the appointment of the special administrator.
A determination under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
The Registrar may make a determination under subsection (1) only if the Registrar is satisfied that making the determination is in the best interests of the corporation.
A determination under subsection (1) must be included in the special administrator’s appointment.

section.heading: Powers of officers can only be exercised by, or with the consent of, special administrator

content.p: While an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is under special administration, a person (other than the special administrator) cannot perform or exercise, and must not purport to perform or exercise, a function or power as an officer of the corporation.
Penalty: 25 penalty units or imprisonment for 6 months, or both.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the extent to which the performance or exercise, or purported performance or exercise, is with the special administrator’s written approval.
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matter in subsection (2) (see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code).

Subsection (1) does not apply to the extent to which the person is performing or exercising, or purporting to perform or exercise, a function or power as restructuring practitioner for a restructuring plan made by the corporation under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act).
Note: A defendant bears an evidential burden in relation to the matter in subsection (2A) (see subsection 13.3(3) of the Criminal Code).
An offence against subsection (1) is an offence of strict liability.
Note: For strict liability, see section 6.1 of the Criminal Code.
Subsection (1) does not remove an officer of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation from his or her office.
Section 496-15 does not limit the generality of subsection (1) of this section.
This section has effect despite:
Part 5.2 of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 516-1 of this Act); and
Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act).

Note: This means that a receiver, or an administrator appointed under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act), cannot exercise any powers without the approval of the special administrator.
Despite subsection (6), this section does not affect the validity of anything that a person who is:
a receiver, or a receiver and manager, of property of the corporation; or
an administrator of the corporation appointed under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act;
does after the special administration begins and on or before the day on which the Registrar complies with subsection 493-1(4) in relation to the special administration.

section.heading: Only special administrator can deal with corporation’s property

content.p: This section applies if:
an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration purports to enter into; or
a person purports to enter into, on behalf of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration;
a transaction or dealing affecting property of the corporation.
The transaction or dealing is void unless:
the special administrator entered into it on the corporation’s behalf; or
the special administrator consented to it in writing before it was entered into; or
it was entered into under an order of the Court.
Subsection (2) does not apply to a payment made:
by an Australian ADI out of an account kept by the corporation with the ADI; and
in good faith and in the ordinary course of the ADI’s banking business; and
after the special administration begins and on or before the day on which the Registrar complies with subsection 493-1(4) in relation to the special administration.
Subsection (2) does not apply to a transaction or dealing affecting property of the corporation if:
the corporation has made a restructuring plan under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act) that has not terminated; and
the restructuring plan specifies how the property is to be dealt with; and
the transaction or dealing complies with the terms of the restructuring plan.
Subsection (2) has effect subject to an order that the Court makes after the purported transaction or dealing.
If, because of subsection (2), the transaction or dealing is void, or would be void apart from subsection (4), an officer or employee of the corporation who:
purported to enter into the transaction or dealing on the corporation’s behalf; or
was in any other way, by act or omission, directly or indirectly, knowingly concerned in, or party to, the transaction or dealing;
contravenes this subsection.
Penalty: 25 penalty units or imprisonment for 6 months, or both.
This section has effect despite:
Part 5.2 of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 516-1 of this Act); and
Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act).

Note: This means that a receiver, or an administrator appointed under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act), cannot enter into any transactions or dealings without the consent of the special administrator or an order of the Court.
Despite subsection (6), this section does not affect the validity of anything that a person who is:
a receiver, or a receiver and manager, of property of the corporation; or
an administrator of the corporation appointed under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act;
does after the special administration begins and on or before the day on which the Registrar complies with subsection 493-1(4) in relation to the special administration.

section.heading: Order for compensation where officer involved in void transaction

content.p: If:

(a) a court finds that a person committed an offence constituted by a contravention of subsection 496-15(5) (including such an offence that is taken to have been committed because of section 11.2 or 11.2A of the Criminal Code); and
the court is satisfied that the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation or another person has suffered loss or damage because of the act or omission constituting the offence;
the court may (whether or not it imposes a penalty) order the first-mentioned person to pay compensation to the corporation or other person, as the case may be, of such amount as the order specifies.
An order under subsection (1) may be enforced as if it were a judgment of the court.

The power of a court under section 576-1 to relieve a person from liability as mentioned in that section extends to relieving a person from liability to be ordered under this section to pay compensation.

division.heading: Function, duties and powers of special administrator

content.p: While an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is under special administration, the special administrator is responsible for the conduct of the affairs of the corporation.
While an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is under special administration, the special administrator:
has control of the corporation’s business, property and affairs; and
may carry on that business and manage that property and those affairs; and
may terminate or dispose of all or part of that business, and may dispose of any of that property; and
may engage or discharge employees on behalf of the corporation; and
may perform any function, and exercise any power, that:
the corporation; or
any of the corporation’s officers; or
the corporation’s members;
could perform or exercise if the corporation were not under special administration.
This subsection has effect even if the offices of the corporation’s officers are not vacated on the appointment of the special administrator.
To avoid doubt and without limiting paragraph (1)(e), the special administrator may perform any function and exercise any power that the corporation has as trustee.
Without limiting subsection (1), the special administrator may do the following:
change the corporation’s constitution;
admit a person as a member of the corporation;
remove a person as a member of the corporation;
appoint a person as a director or secretary of the corporation;
terminate a person’s appointment as a director or secretary of the corporation;
terminate a person’s appointment as contact person for the corporation.

In changing the corporation’s constitution, the special administrator does not have to comply with paragraph 69-5(1)(a) (special resolution), section 69-15 (satisfying extra requirements in constitution) or section 69-20 (corporation to lodge copy of changes).
Note: The special administrator must still lodge a copy of the change under section 69-25.

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration

content.p: The following provisions of the Corporations Act apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration:
Division 6 of Part 5.3A (other than section 440A);
Division 7 of Part 5.3A;
Division 8 (other than section 442A) of Part 5.3A;
Division 9 of Part 5.3A;

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of the provisions referred to in paragraphs (a) to (d);
the regulations made under that Act for the purposes of the provisions of that Act referred to in paragraphs (a) to (e).
Those provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

content.p: The provisions of the Corporations Act mentioned in subsection (1) apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is under special administration:
only to the extent to which they are capable of applying to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
with the modifications specified in the regulations.
Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph (3)(b) must not:
increase, or have the effect of increasing, the maximum penalty for any offence; or
widen, or have the effect of widening, the scope of any offence.

division.heading: Special administrator to report to Registrar

content.p: A special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation must give the Registrar such information as the Registrar requires from time to time.

section.heading: Termination of appointment of special administrator

content.p: The appointment of a special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation terminates if:
the period for which the special administrator is appointed ends; or
the special administrator dies; or
a liquidator for the corporation is appointed; or
the corporation is being wound up; or
the special administrator resigns the appointment by notice in writing to the Registrar; or
the Registrar terminates the special administrator’s appointment under subsection (4); or
the Registrar terminates the special administration under section 487-20.
Note: The termination of the appointment of the special administrator does not necessarily terminate the special administration. For when the special administration ceases, see section 487-25.

Subject to subsection (3), the special administrator’s resignation under paragraph (1)(e) takes effect at the end of the period of 28 days after the day on which the special administrator gives the notice to the Registrar.

The Registrar may, on application by the special administrator, determine in writing that the special administrator’s resignation is to take effect before the end of the period of 28 days referred to in subsection (2).

The Registrar may, by notice in writing to the special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation, terminate the special administrator’s appointment if satisfied that it is appropriate to do so.
Without limiting subsection 505-1(4), the Registrar may be satisfied that it is appropriate to terminate the special administrator’s appointment if the Registrar is satisfied that:
it is no longer necessary for the corporation to be under special administration; or
the special administrator has a material personal interest in a matter related to the special administration of the corporation; or
the special administrator’s performance is not satisfactory; or
the special administrator has contravened a provision of this Act; or
it would be appropriate in the circumstances to replace the special administrator with another special administrator with different skills, experience or qualifications.

section.heading: Registrar to appoint new special administrator in certain circumstances

content.p: If the appointment of a special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation terminates, the Registrar must, as soon as practicable after the termination of the appointment, appoint another person as special administrator for the corporation.
Subsection (1) does not apply if the Registrar is satisfied that it is no longer necessary for the corporation to be under special administration.

division.heading: Transition to normal control of the corporation’s affairs at end of special administration

section.heading: Special administrator to ensure that there will be directors when corporation ceases to be under special administration

content.p: The special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation must ensure that, immediately after the special administration of the corporation ends, there will be:
directors of the corporation who can assume control of the corporation’s affairs; and
a secretary for the corporation if it is registered as a large corporation; and
a contact person for the corporation if it is registered as a small or medium corporation.
Note: There are a number of different ways in which there can be directors who can assume control of the corporation’s affairs when the special administration ends. For example:

the offices of the directors may not have been vacated when the special administrator was appointed and some or all of those directors may remain in office at the end of the special administration; or

the special administrator may have exercised his or her power to appoint directors under subsection 499-5(3) and some or all of the appointees may remain in office at the end of the special administration; or

persons may, at a general meeting of the members of the corporation called by the special administrator under section 508-5, have been elected as directors to assume control of the corporation’s affairs when the special administration ends.
Subsection (1) does not apply if:
the corporation is to cease to be under special administration because a liquidator for the corporation is appointed; or

the corporation is to cease to be under special administration so that an administrator may be appointed, or may resume exercising powers, under the Corporations Act administration provisions (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act).

section.heading: Election of directors to take over affairs of corporation when corporation ceases to be under special administration

content.p: The special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation may conduct an election to elect directors to assume control of the corporation’s affairs immediately after the corporation ceases to be under special administration.
Without limiting subsection (1), the election may be conducted:
at a general meeting of the members of the corporation; or
by postal ballot.
A person may be elected as a director under this section if the person gives the corporation a signed consent to act as a director of the corporation before being elected.
The persons elected:
become the directors of the corporation immediately after the corporation ceases to be under special administration; and
continue to hold office until the end of the next AGM of the corporation unless removed from office before then.
The special administrator for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is to receive such remuneration (if any) as the Registrar determines in writing.
A determination under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
Subject to subsection (4), the special administrator’s remuneration, charges and expenses are to be borne by the Commonwealth.
The Registrar:
may determine, in writing, that some or all of the special administrator’s remuneration, charges or expenses are to be borne by the corporation or a related body corporate; and

may charge some or all of the remuneration, charges or expenses referred to in paragraph (a) on the property of the corporation or a related body corporate in such order of priority in relation to any existing charges on that property as the Registrar thinks fit.
This section does not apply to a special administrator who is an APS employee or a Commonwealth officer.
(5A) Subsection 73(2) of the Personal Property Securities Act 2009 applies to a charge created in accordance with paragraph (4)(b).

Note 1: The effect of this subsection is that the priority between a charge created in accordance with paragraph (4)(b) and a security interest to which the Personal Property Securities Act 2009 applies is to be determined in accordance with this Act rather than the Personal Property Securities Act 2009.

Note 2: Subsection 73(2) of the Personal Property Securities Act 2009 applies to charges that arise after the commencement of subsection (5A) (which is the registration commencement time within the meaning of the Personal Property Securities Act 2009).
In this section:
Commonwealth officer includes a person who:
is in the service or employment of the Commonwealth or an authority of the Commonwealth; or
holds or performs the duties of any office or position under a law of the Commonwealth; or
is a member of the Australian Defence Force.

part.heading: Receivers, and other controllers, of property of corporations

division.heading: Receivers, and other controllers, of property of corporations

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act receiver provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations

content.p: The Corporations Act receiver provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation
an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

content.p: The Corporations Act receiver provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation:
only to the extent to which they are capable of applying to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
with the modifications specified in the regulations.
Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph (2)(b) must not:
increase, or have the effect of increasing, the maximum penalty for any offence; or
widen, or have the effect of widening, the scope of any offence.
In this Act:
Corporations Act receiver provisions means:
Part 5.2 of the Corporations Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2, 5.8, 5.9 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of Part 5.2 of that Act; and
the regulations made under that Act for the purposes of Part 5.2 of that Act and the provisions referred to in paragraph (b).

part.heading: Administration of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation’s affairs with a view to executing a deed of corporation arrangement

division.heading: Administration of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation’s affairs with a view to executing a deed of corporation arrangement

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act administration provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations

content.p: The Corporations Act administration provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation
registered office or document access address

content.p: The Corporations Act administration provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation:
only to the extent to which they are capable of applying to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
with the modifications specified in the regulations.
Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph (2)(b) must not:
increase, or have the effect of increasing, the maximum penalty for any offence; or
widen, or have the effect of widening, the scope of any offence.
In this Act:
Corporations Act administration provisions means:
Part 5.3A of, and Schedule 2 to, the Corporations Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2, 5.8, 5.9 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of Part 5.3A of, and Schedule 2 to, that Act; and
the regulations and rules made under that Act for the purposes of Part 5.3A of, and Schedule 2 to, that Act and the provisions referred to in paragraph (b).

section.heading: Administrator’s capacity to act as trustee

content.p: To avoid doubt, an administrator appointed under the Corporations Act administration provisions (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act) may, under those provisions as applied, perform any function and exercise any power that the corporation has as trustee.

section.heading: Corporations Act administrator cannot be appointed if special administrator appointed

content.p: An administrator of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation cannot be appointed under section 436A, 436B or 436C of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1) if:
the corporation is under special administration under Part 11-2; or
the Registrar:
has given the corporation a notice under subsection 487-10(1); and
has not given the corporation a notice under subsection 487-10(5).
Paragraph (1)(b) does not apply if the Registrar has consented in writing to the appointment of the administrator under that section of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act).
A consent under subsection (2) to the appointment of an administrator is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Effect of appointment of special administrator on Corporations Act administrator

content.p: This section deals with the situation in which:

(a) an administrator of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation (the Corporations Act administrator) is appointed under section 436A, 436B or 436C of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act); and
while that appointment continues, a special administrator for the corporation is appointed under Part 11-2.
Note: Section 496-10 deals with the effect of the special administrator’s appointment on the Corporations Act administrator’s powers.
The Court may order that the administration of the corporation under Part 5.3A of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 521-1 of this Act) is to end.
The order may be made on the application of:
the Registrar; or
the special administrator for the corporation; or
any other interested person.
The order may be made subject to conditions.

part.heading: Restructuring of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

division.heading: Restructuring of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act restructuring provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations

content.p: The Corporations Act restructuring provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

content.p: The Corporations Act restructuring provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation:
only to the extent to which they are capable of applying to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
with the modifications specified in the regulations.
Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph (2)(b) must not:
increase, or have the effect of increasing, the maximum penalty for any offence; or
widen, or have the effect of widening, the scope of any offence.
In this Act:
Corporations Act restructuring provisions means:
Part 5.3B of, and Schedule 2 to, the Corporations Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2, 5.8, 5.9 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of Part 5.3B of, and Schedule 2 to, that Act; and
the regulations and rules made under that Act for the purposes of Part 5.3B of, and Schedule 2 to, that Act and the provisions referred to in paragraph (b).

section.heading: Corporations Act restructuring practitioner cannot be appointed if special administrator appointed

content.p: A restructuring practitioner for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation cannot be appointed under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act) if:
the corporation is under special administration under Part 11-2; or
the Registrar:
has given the corporation a notice under subsection 487-10(1); and
has not given the corporation a notice under subsection 487-10(5).

Paragraph (1)(b) does not apply if the Registrar has consented in writing to the appointment of the restructuring practitioner under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act).
A consent under subsection (2) to the appointment of a restructuring practitioner is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Effect of appointment of special administrator—Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation under restructuring

content.p: If:
a restructuring practitioner for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation is appointed under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act); and
while that appointment continues, a special administrator for the corporation is appointed under Part 11-2; and
at the time the special administrator is appointed, the corporation has not made a restructuring plan;
the restructuring of the corporation under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act) ends on the day on which the special administrator is appointed.

section.heading: Effect of appointment of special administrator—Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation subject to restructuring plan

content.p: This section applies if:
an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation makes a restructuring plan under Part 5.3B of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 522-1 of this Act); and
before the plan terminates, a special administrator for the corporation is appointed under Part 11-2.
The Court may order that the restructuring plan is to terminate.
The order may be made on the application of:
the Registrar; or
the special administrator for the corporation; or
any other interested person.
The order may be made subject to conditions.
Effect of termination of restructuring plan

If the Court orders that the restructuring plan is to terminate, any admissible debt or claim that has not been dealt with in accordance with the restructuring plan is taken to be due and payable on the business day after the day on which the termination occurs.
In this section:
admissible debt or claim has the same meaning as in the Corporations Regulations 2001.
The Court may order that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation be wound up.
The order may only be made on the grounds set out in section 526-5.
The order may only be made on an application made in accordance with section 526-15.

section.heading: Grounds for Court ordered winding up

content.p: The following are the grounds on which an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation may be wound up:
the corporation has by special resolution resolved that it be wound up by the Court;
the business or operations of the corporation were not commenced within 1 year after its registration or have been suspended for a continuous period of 1 year;
the corporation has ceased to satisfy a requirement for registration imposed by section 141-5, 141-10 or 141-15;
section 26-15 precludes the continued registration of the corporation;
the officers of the corporation have acted in the affairs of the corporation:
in their own interests rather than in the interests of the members of the corporation as a whole; or
in a way that appears to be unfair or unjust to the members of the corporation;
the affairs of the corporation are being conducted in a way that is:
oppressive; or
unfairly prejudicial to, or unfairly discriminatory against, a member or members of the corporation; or
contrary to the interests of the members of the corporation as a whole;
an act or omission, or a proposed act or omission, by or on behalf of the corporation was or would be:
oppressive; or
unfairly prejudicial to, or unfairly discriminatory against, a member or members of the corporation; or
contrary to the interests of the members as a whole;
a resolution, or a proposed resolution, of a class of members of the corporation, was or would be:
oppressive; or
unfairly prejudicial to, or unfairly discriminatory against, a member or members of the corporation; or
contrary to the interests of the members of the corporation as a whole;
the corporation is insolvent;
the directors of the corporation have failed to comply with a notice that the Registrar has given the directors under section 439-20;
the corporation has failed, for a prescribed period, to lodge any financial or other reports required to be lodged by Part 7-3;
by reason of the complexity or magnitude of the activities of the corporation, it is inappropriate that it continue to be registered under this Act;
the Court is satisfied that it is in the interests of:
the public; or
the corporation’s members; or
the corporation’s creditors;
that the corporation should be wound up;
the Court is satisfied that it is just and equitable that the corporation be wound up.

section.heading: Acts etc. done to comply with Native Title legislation requirement

content.p: Paragraph 526-5(e) or (f) does not apply to an officer of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation that is a registered native title body corporate merely because of doing (or refraining from doing) a particular act if the officer does (or refrains from doing) the act:
in good faith; and
with the belief that doing (or refraining from doing) the act is necessary to ensure that the corporation complies with a Native Title legislation obligation.

Paragraph 526-5(g) does not apply to an act or omission, or a proposed act or omission, by or on behalf of a corporation that is a registered native title body corporate, if the act or omission, or the proposed act or omission, was done:
in good faith; and
with the belief that the doing of the act or omission, or the proposed act or omission, is necessary to ensure that the corporation complies with a Native Title legislation obligation.

Paragraph 526-5(h) does not apply to a resolution, or a proposed resolution, of a class of members of a corporation that is a registered native title body corporate, if the resolution, or proposed resolution, was made:
in good faith; and
with the belief that the making of the resolution, or proposed resolution, is necessary to ensure that the corporation complies with a Native Title legislation obligation.

section.heading: Who may apply to court for winding up order

content.p: Any one or more of the following may apply to the Court for an order that an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation be wound up:
the corporation;
a creditor of the corporation (even if the creditor is a secured creditor or is only a contingent or prospective creditor);
a member of the corporation;
a director of the corporation;
a contributory of the corporation;
a liquidator, or a provisional liquidator, of the corporation;
a special administrator of the corporation;
the Registrar.
This subsection has effect subject to subsections (2), (3), (4) and (5).

The Registrar is the only person who may apply for an order that the corporation be wound up if the grounds on which the winding up is applied for are, or include, grounds referred to in any of the following:
paragraph 526-5(j) (failure to comply with a section 439-20 notice);
paragraph 526-5(k) (failure to lodge reports);
paragraph 526-5(l) (complexity or magnitude of corporation’s activities).
If the corporation is under special administration only the Registrar or the special administrator may apply for an order that the corporation be wound up.

An application by any of the following, or by persons including any of the following, for an order that the corporation be wound up because it is insolvent may only be made with the leave of the Court:
a person who is a creditor only because of a contingent or prospective debt;
a contributory;
a director;
the Registrar.
The court must not hear an application by a person being, or persons including, a contingent or prospective creditor of the corporation for an order to wind up the corporation unless and until:
such security for costs has been given as the Court thinks reasonable; and
a prima facie case for winding up the corporation has been established to the Court’s satisfaction.
Except as permitted by this section, a person is not entitled to apply for an order to wind up an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation.
Subject to subsection (5), an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation may be wound up voluntarily if the members of the corporation in general meeting so resolve by special resolution.
An Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation cannot resolve that it be wound up voluntarily if:
the corporation is under special administration under Part 11-2; or
the Registrar:
has given the corporation a notice under subsection 487-10(1); and
has not given the corporation a notice under subsection 487-10(5).
Paragraph (2)(b) does not apply if the Registrar has consented in writing to the voluntary winding up of the corporation.
A consent given by the Registrar under subsection (3) is not a legislative instrument
Except with the leave of the Court, an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation cannot resolve that it be wound up voluntarily if:
an application has been made to the Court for the corporation to be wound up on the ground that it is insolvent; or
the Court has ordered that the corporation be wound up on the ground that it is insolvent (whether or not the order was made on such an application).

If an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation passes a resolution for the voluntary winding up of the corporation, the corporation must, within 28 days after the passing of a resolution, lodge with the Registrar:
a notice in the approved form of the passing of the resolution; and
a copy of the resolution.
Penalty: 5 penalty units.
Subsection (6) is an offence of strict liability.
Note: For strict liability, see section 6.1 of the Criminal Code.
(8) The Registrar must, within 21 days after the lodging of a notice under subsection (6), publish in the Gazette a notice of the passing of the resolution to which the notice relates.

section.heading: Distribution of surplus assets in winding up by Court

content.p: This section applies if:
surplus assets remain on the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
the winding up is a winding up by the Court.

If the corporation’s constitution includes provisions for the distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in the event of the corporation’s being wound up, the Court or the liquidator must distribute those assets in accordance with those provisions. This subsection has effect subject to subsection (4).
Note: The liquidator may have powers in relation to the distribution of the surplus under section 488 of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 526-35 of this Act).
If:
the corporation’s constitution does not include provisions for the distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in the event of the corporation’s being wound up; and
the members of the corporation pass a special resolution relating to the distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation;
the Court or the liquidator must distribute those assets in accordance with that special resolution. This subsection has effect subject to subsection (4).
Note: The liquidator may have powers in relation to the distribution of the surplus under section 488 of the Corporations Act (as applied by section 526-35 of this Act).
If:
a Judge of the Court considers that a distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in accordance with:
the provisions of the corporation’s constitution in accordance with subsection (2); or
a special resolution in accordance with subsection (3);
would not be just; or
no such provisions exist and such a special resolution has not been passed;
the Judge must make such orders for the distribution of those assets as, having regard to the objects of the corporation, he or she considers just.

section.heading: Distribution of surplus assets in voluntary winding up

content.p: This section applies if:
surplus assets remain on the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
the winding up is a voluntary winding up.

If the corporation’s constitution includes provisions for the distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in the event of the corporation’s being wound up, the liquidator must distribute those assets in accordance with those provisions. This subsection has effect subject to subsection (5).
If:
the corporation’s constitution does not include provisions for the distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in the event of the corporation’s being wound up; and
the members of the corporation pass a special resolution relating to the distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation;
the liquidator must distribute those assets in accordance with that special resolution. This subsection has effect subject to subsection (5).
If:
the liquidator considers that a distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in accordance with:
the provisions of the corporation’s constitution in accordance with subsection (2); or
a special resolution in accordance with subsection (3);
would not be just; or
no such provisions exist and such a special resolution has not been passed;
the liquidator must apply to a Judge of the Court for an order under subsection (5).
If:
the Judge considers that a distribution of the surplus assets of the corporation in accordance with:
the provisions of the corporation’s constitution in accordance with subsection (1); or
a special resolution in accordance with subsection (2);
would not be just; or
no such provisions exist and such a special resolution has not been passed;
the Judge must make such orders for the distribution of those assets as, having regard to the objects of the corporation, he or she considers just.

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act winding up provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations

content.p: The Corporations Act winding up provisions apply to the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation
any distribution by the corporation to its members (whether of capital or income)
civil penalty order (within the meaning of this Act)
civil penalty provision (within the meaning of this Act)

content.p: Note: Item 4 is relevant to the operation of subsection 588G(1A) of the Corporations Act.
The Corporations Act winding up provisions apply to the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation:
only to the extent to which they are capable of applying to the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation; and
with the modifications specified in the regulations.
Regulations made for the purposes of paragraph (2)(b) must not:
increase, or have the effect of increasing, the maximum penalty for any offence; or
widen, or have the effect of widening, the scope of any offence.
In this Act:
Corporations Act winding up provisions means:
Parts 5.4, 5.4B, 5.5, 5.6, 5.7B, 5.8, 5.8A and 5.9 of, and Schedule 2 to, the Corporations Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of the provisions referred to in paragraph (a); and
the regulations and rules made under that Act for the purposes of the provisions of that Act referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b);
but does not include the excluded winding up provisions of that Act.
excluded winding up provisions of the Corporations Act means:
section 459A of that Act (which deals with the court’s power to order a winding up); and
section 459B of that Act (which deals with insolvency as a ground for winding up); and
section 459P of that Act (which deals with who may apply for a winding up on the grounds of insolvency); and
section 490 of that Act (which deals with when a resolution for voluntary winding up may be passed); and
section 491 of that Act (which deal with the resolution for a voluntary winding up).

section.heading: Application of Corporations Act pre-winding up provisions

content.p: The Corporations Act pre-winding up provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation

content.p: Note: This section is intended to apply to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations some provisions of the Corporations Act that are capable of operating before a winding up commences (or even whether or not a winding up ever occurs). Section 526-35 only applies provisions of the Corporations Act to a winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation.
This section has effect without limiting section 526-35.
In this Act:
Corporations Act pre-winding up provisions means:
section 459C, Divisions 2 and 3 of Part 5.4 and section 459Q of the Corporations Act; and
section 487 of that Act; and
section 494 of that Act; and
section 570 of that Act; and
Division 9 of Part 5.6 of that Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2, 5.8 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of the provisions referred to in paragraphs (a) to (e); and
the regulations made under that Act for the purposes of the provisions of that Act referred to in paragraphs (a) to (e) and the provisions referred to in paragraph (f).

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act insolvent trading and creditor-defeating disposition provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations

content.p: The Corporations Act insolvent trading and creditor-defeating disposition provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation
any distribution by the corporation to its members (whether of capital or income)
civil penalty order (within the meaning of this Act)
civil penalty provision (within the meaning of this Act)

content.p: Note: Although section 526-35 applies the provisions of Part 5.7B to the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation, the insolvent trading and creditor-defeating disposition provisions are capable of applying independently of there being a winding up. This section ensures, for example, that a director of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation commits an offence if the corporation trades while insolvent (regardless of whether winding up proceedings are ever commenced).
This section has effect without limiting section 526-35.
In this Act:
Corporations Act insolvent trading and creditor-defeating disposition provisions means:
Divisions 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Part 5.7B of the Corporations Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2 and 9.4 and Schedule 3 but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of the Divisions referred to in paragraph (a); and
the regulations made under that Act for the purposes of the Divisions of that Act referred to in paragraph (a) and the provisions referred to in paragraph (b).

section.heading: Sections 588G, 588GAB and 588GAC of Corporations Act prevail over conflicting Native Title legislation obligations

content.p: In the event of a conflict between:
the duty of a director of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation to ensure that the corporation comply with its Native Title legislation obligations; and
the director’s duty in relation to the corporation under section 588G, 588GAB or 588GAC of the Corporations Act as applied by section 531-1 of this Act;
the director’s duty under section 588G, 588GAB or 588GAC of the Corporations Act as so applied prevails, and the director is released from the first-mentioned duty, to the extent of the conflict.

The corporation is released from the duty to comply with its Native Title legislation obligations to the extent that complying with them would place a director of the corporation in breach of his or her duty in relation to the corporation under section 588G, 588GAB or 588GAC of the Corporations Act as so applied.

section.heading: Applying Corporations Act employees’ entitlements provisions to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporations

content.p: The Corporations Act employees’ entitlements provisions apply to an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation as if the following substitutions were made:

tr.td: an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation
civil penalty order (within the meaning of this Act)

content.p: Note: Although section 526-35 applies the provisions of Part 5.8A to the winding up of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation, the employees’ entitlements provisions are capable of applying independently of there being a winding up. This section ensures, for example, that a person will commit an offence (under the applied section 596AB) if the person enters into an agreement to defeat the entitlements of employees of an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation (regardless of whether winding up proceedings are ever commenced).
This section has effect without limiting section 526-35.
In this Act:
Corporations Act employees’ entitlements provisions means:
Part 5.8A of the Corporations Act; and

the other provisions of that Act (including Parts 1.2 and 9.4 and Schedule 3, but not including Parts 1.1, 1.1A and 9.4A) to the extent to which they relate to the operation of the Part referred to in paragraph (a); and
the regulations made under that Act for the purposes of Part 5.8A of that Act and the provisions referred to in paragraph (b).

chapter.heading: Transfer of registration, deregistration and unclaimed property

part.heading: Transfer of registration to another system

content.p: An Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander corporation may transfer its registration to registration under a law of the Commonwealth, a State or a Territory by:
